scores.critique: Most literal reading of SPEC §5.3 (all four tools + submit_edl, tool-use agent, in-tool validation loop) and the most layered failure handling (nudges, max_tokens retry at 20k, strict->non-strict retry, PlanError with resumable job, opt-in [fallback] EDL). But it is the expensive, slow design: its own estimate is ~15 iterations and $0.7-0.9 per 10-min video with DEFAULT_LIMITS of 24 iterations / $3. Each Opus 5.5 iteration with adaptive thinking is ~10-30 s, so 10-15 round-trips is 3-7 min for the planner alone, on top of ingest/understand/cut -- it does not reliably fit the SPEC §8 5-minute guideline. Cache layout is correct (3 explicit + automatic breakpoint, name-sorted tools, frozen system, deterministic overview) but the cost is dominated by output/thinking tokens across many turns (15 x 2k x $20/M = $0.60), which caching cannot help; the strict retry also forces a full cache rebuild. No wall-clock cap. The strict-mode retry keys on error-message text, which the notes say never to do. 20 files is a lot of surface for a stage-3 MVP.

Best cost/latency profile by a wide margin: one deterministic ~13-15k-token pack, structured output via betaZodOutputFormat, happy path = 1 request (~$0.15-0.18, ~1-2 min; the stated 30-60 s is optimistic for 3-5k output tokens incl. thinking), repair/frames = 2 requests, hard cap 12. Cache plan is sound (tools+system shared across jobs, pack cached per job, repair/revise re-read at $0.2/M) and the ref grammar (p12/s3) makes the §5.3 boundary rule true by construction, which removes the whole validate->resubmit round-trip class. Deviates from SPEC's 'Claude with tool use' in spirit (tools declared but discouraged; validate_edl not used on the happy path), and the pack-only approach limits exploration. Real weakness: refs restrict cut points to whole whisper phrases or ffmpeg scene edges; long phrases (10-15 s) make 'dynamic' 2-6 s clips and exact 30 s targets hard, and t-refs are rejected in plan mode -- graft gap boundaries (see below). Core unverified combination (output_config.format + client tools in one request) is well mitigated by feature detection and --no-tools. Agent SDK option names it cites (effort, thinking, outputFormat, resume, structured_output) do exist in the installed sdk.d.ts. Cost accounting is the most granular (one cost.json entry per request).

Balanced middle: five tools, three acceptance paths (submit_edl, JSON-in-text, last valid draft), repair turns, and the only design with an explicit wall-clock budget (maxWallMs 240 s via AbortSignal) and USD cap ($1) tied to SPEC §8. Context block is the leanest (phrases without words, ~8-12k tokens). Still ~8 requests and 6-10 tool calls per plan (~$0.35-0.45, 2-4 min), so it is roughly 2x context-first's cost and latency, and the 240 s cap can truncate legitimate runs on talky 10-min videos (falls to last_valid/partial). Enabling fallbacks:'default' on every request is a cost-predictability risk: a rescued turn runs on another model without thinking, misses the model-scoped cache, and -- since PRICES only has claude-opus-5-5 -- is logged as usd 0 'unpriced'. Repair replays runner.params.messages into a new runner (thinking-binding risk acknowledged). Image token estimate (0.5-1k per 640px frame) is ~2-3x too high. FIELD_STAGES diff->stage mapping and the cache-health CLI warning are the best stage-5/ops ideas in the set.

scores.critique: The most literal reading of SPEC §5.3/§9 (a tool-use agent with the four tools plus a strict submit_edl) and the most layered failure handling: validation+auto-repair inside the tool protocol, append-only nudges, one max_tokens retry at 20k (still under the 21333 non-streaming guard), strict->non-strict retry, per-tool and USD budgets, refusal handling, honest [fallback] EDL only on opt-in. I verified against the installed BetaToolRunner.js that its generateToolResponse()+break trick is sound (the public method uses the in-flight #message and caches in #toolResponse, so tools never run twice). Costs of the approach: ~20 new files, a loop policy split between loop.ts and anthropic.ts, and no wall-clock cap — 24 iterations of Opus 5.5 at ~20-40 s each plus the $3 default budget make the SPEC §8 '10-min video in <=5 min' guideline the most likely to be missed; its own estimate ($0.7-0.9/plan) is 3-5x the others. The agent-sdk backend (the only one the user can run today) is specified for tools/images but the nudge/round policy is never described for it. Revise reuses the full loop (expensive) and frameForScene keeps the scene-index==shot-index coupling that a Gemini provider with merged scenes will silently break (shot_001.jpg exists but is the wrong frame); the design at least documents the assumption and proposes a ScenesSchema.frame field.

Strongest engineering idea of the three: the model never emits seconds — clips are phrase/scene refs resolved by the harness, so SPEC's 'phrase or scene boundary' rule holds by construction and whole error classes (timestamp arithmetic, mid-word cuts except at scene edges) disappear; one pure resolveDraft() backs the harness check, validate_edl and revise. Happy path is 1 call (~$0.15-0.30, 30-60 s), repairs are append-only, and the backend contract is two methods (start/continue) with the entire state machine in a no-I/O loop.ts — the best offline-testability and the cleanest surface for a maintainer. Its Agent SDK path is well matched: outputFormat json_schema, resume, structured_output and error_max_structured_output_retries all exist in the installed sdk.d.ts (I checked lines 1980/2092/5860/5731) and the CLI implements structured output as an end-turn tool, so MCP tools + structured output is native there. Pack carries no frame paths at all, so a Gemini vision swap touches nothing in the planner; revise is cheap and versioned (edl.vN.json, revise.json) though draftFromEdl's t-ref grammar for hand-edited edges is the one intricate piece. Weak points that cost it robustness: the Anthropic-API happy path bets on output_config.format + client tools in one request, which the notes never confirm (mitigated by feature-detect and --no-tools, but if the API rejects it, preview_frame vanishes on that backend); spec conformance is weaker in spirit since the four SPEC tools are declared 'optional/redundant in FULL mode'; the count check relies on the model's self-reported brief; auto-selection keys on claude.exe being resolvable (via require.resolve in an ESM project, which needs createRequire) rather than on a login credential; there is no wall-clock limit; and it hard-codes unsourced prices for claude-opus-5 / claude-opus-4-8.

Pragmatic and well-bounded: one Planner class serves plan and revise, a BudgetTracker enforces USD, iterations, repairs, tool calls, preview frames and a 240 s wall clock via AbortSignal (the only design that takes SPEC §8's time guideline seriously), submit_edl/validate_edl are exempt from the tool cap so the model can always finish, and three acceptance paths (submit_edl -> JSON in final text -> last valid validate_edl candidate) plus repair turns make a hard failure rare. diff.ts with FIELD_STAGES (clips->cut/design/render, captions/titles->design/render) is the most useful stage-5 artifact of all three designs, and the honest '[mock]' heuristic planner gives an LLM-free end-to-end path for demos and CI. It is also the most robust against the Windows/Cyrillic-path unknown (cwd os.tmpdir() + CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME) and uses the right auth signal (credentials file or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN). What holds it back for this user: the agent-sdk backend — the only one usable on a subscription today — is deliberately degraded (preview_frame text-only, stateless repair via a fresh query, --effort ignored even though sdk.d.ts has effort/thinking options), so 9:16 framing checks are weakest exactly where they will run. Server-side fallbacks are on by default (a refusal silently continues on a different model without Opus 5.5 thinking, at other rates). The final-text JSON extraction path is a soft contract.
